utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Although we have curtain drawn down, we are in private session -- no, in public session. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you for the reminder that we are currently in open session. I'd like to address a number of scheduling matters but I think it's probably best done in private session, given the number of factors involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. May the Court proceed into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, with respect to the recently filed 58th motion for finding of disclosure violation and for sanctions, Witness KDZ052, the Chamber observes that this motion pertains to an upcoming witness, KDZ052, who is scheduled to testify next week. So can the Prosecution orally respond to this motion during the course of today? And I would like the Prosecution to identify in its response why the transcript of the testimony referred to in the motion was not disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We were in the process of preparing an expedited written submission, Mr. President. We had expected to file today, if that's acceptable. We can proceed if the Court would prefer an oral response. We are always at the court's disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will go back to private session and continue with the evidence. I was mistaken. We can continue in public session. Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to be excused so I can go and continue the preparation for the -- KDZ601, and we being a team in the Prosecution, Mr. Tieger is fully briefed to be able to proceed in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies, good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of a massacre against Serbs at Borike by the Muslim forces on the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Zlatni Do in your statement dated 12th of January, 1994, in paragraph 2. I do believe we can find it in your amalgamated statement as well. Do you know that on the 22nd of May, or perhaps or most probably on the 20th of May, a Serb policeman was killed -- rather, it was on 21 May. Drazenko Mihajlovic, whilst he was patrolling an area which belonged to the Serb municipality in the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you most certainly do not know that they refused to hand over his body and said that they would not do so before they had killed ten more Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know to which constituent unit was your municipality supposed to belong under the Cutileiro Plan and the Vance Owen and the Owen Stoltenberg plans, the latter of which I agreed to, including the contact group plan?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that without a war and armed conflict, whatever the prevailing variant, your municipality and other municipalities of the valley -- of the Drina valley would belong to the federation unit, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we get to paragraph 54, you will see what the relevance is. Can we now look at 1D883 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were Medjedja and Ustipraca close to your municipality and, in fact, did they share a border?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are right next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time of the relevant events, at Ustipraca and Medjedja there were 3.000 Muslim fighters who were trying to link up the Drina valley with Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me which year that was, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely in the months when this particular event took place.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of such a number being present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at this map. If you disregard the yellow line, which indicates the data on Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is a second plotted map by Ambassador Cutileiro, the other one is a bit more favourable for the Serbs, can you find your municipality on this map?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find my way around the map. I know that Rogatica is in the southern part of Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell where Gorazde is and can you see that it does belong to the federation, even here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Usher please help the witness to use the electronic pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you can tell where Foca is, would you place an F there, where Gorazde is, G, Visegrad, V, and then your municipality. You will know how they stand to each other, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what -- what map is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was the first map on offer that I agreed to.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see where Gorazde is? It is still in the federation within the yellow line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do you have to rely on this witness to mark the place Gorazde, Foca and Visegrad? We can all know those places by comparing with other maps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness would be able to mark his municipality, and this in order to indicate that even without a war, the municipality would end up belonging to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can put that question just simply. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. President, and this is an effort to circumvent what would otherwise be an impossible attempt to introduce this document through this witness. We know where the municipality is. Simply identifying the location of the municipality on this map, which the accused is trying to testify about, without benefit of any input from the witness, doesn't add anything to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 54 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you direct me the -- to the proper number of the paragraph? 54 probably has been edited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There might have been a modification done. It's paragraph 55 in the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under A, did you know from personal knowledge that on the 20th of April, 1992, in Jabuka, people were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I spoke to a witness called Mujezinovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us upload his 92 ter statement, para 55, Exhibit P3289. We shouldn't broadcast the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we keep the map for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you not describe the attempt to have you transferred to Olovo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to go to Olovo. When my village came under attack on the 2nd of August, 1992, the 23 of us, among whom there were 14 men and nine women, wanted to go in the direction of Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is how far did you get and why didn't you reach Olovo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't able to reach Olovo because of the fighting that broke out there. On our way there, we came across an ambush and this made it impossible for us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you use this map to indicate the route you took? Is it not true that you moved along the red area, which is the municipality of Sokolac, and that this was Serb held territory and that the confrontation line stood where the yellow line is between Olovo and Sokolac, that it was there and it stayed there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to mark this on the map but I do know and I can explain the route that we took, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't mean much to us unless you can draw it on the map. Very well. So you wouldn't know this from personal knowledge, somebody else told you about the 20th of April, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The survivor who lived in Gorazde and survived the human-shield incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you personally witness the killing at Kalimanic in the month of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't an eyewitness there but there was an eyewitness who survived the killings, who lived in Gorazde and told me the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you would be able to convey his words and what you say are his words, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, did you know about what is listed under C, that in July 1992, in the village of Novoseoci, a large group of Muslims were taken from the village? Were you there? Did you see that happen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see it happen. I heard it. But it was confirmed subsequently since the bodies were exhumed and then buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now, about the incident of the 2nd of August at Kramer Selo, were you there, did you see it with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there, but recently an exhumation was conducted and DNA results are imminent to -- and they would confirm that these were indeed the individuals involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, as for the views described in paragraph 4 and your general political views, were they the result of personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which political events?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the aftermath of the elections, the events in general. Were you following these events?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want me to tell you. Do you want me to say how many seats were won by each of the sides in the elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, in paragraph 12, you referred again to an attack on Kramer Selo. Were you aware of the attacks conducted by the Muslims against the Serb villages in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any Serb village that was torched in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did tell you that I lived in a village which lies in the direction of Sarajevo, so I knew of the Muslim villages that were burned but I didn't know of a single Serb village burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know what the objectives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in relation to your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness, yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I would just like to encourage Mr. Karadzic and the witness to attempt to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your intervention. Please bear in mind that it's important to pause between the question and answers again. Yes, Mr. Witness, can you answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know what the tasks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were. I know for a fact, however, that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina defended the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Witness, that the objective of the Muslim army was the liberation of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that was the goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 11, you refer to the 22nd of May and you mentioned Zlatni Do, and yet you do not know that a policeman by the name of Mihajlovic was killed on the 22nd of May in Zlatni Do and that this marked the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the policeman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder, Your Excellencies, would it be appropriate for you to suggest to the Prosecution that they do not make such all-inclusive and comprehensive statements for witnesses who only have knowledge about one event? The Defence is under pressure to shed light on each and every incident and the witness doesn't know much about any of them, so why doesn't the statement include only this one incident the witness knows of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's another example of improper statement from you. It's for you to cross-examine. You can ask the question. Then if the witness doesn't know, then you should live with it. Please get on with your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated the 12th of January, 1994, you say that there were rumours of the Chetniks taking Muslims prisoner and harassing them and killing them. What exactly are you referring to when you talk of their capture?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question somewhat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, dated the 12th of January, 1992 [as interpreted], in paragraph 2, you say that there were rumours of the Chetniks holding Muslims captive, harassing them and killing them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was harassment, of course. And according to the stories that were going around, there was mistreatment, imprisonment, arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These were rumours, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you're talking about Mehmedagic and Bahtanovic. Are there two Bahtanovics or just one?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is just one Bahtanovic who was arrested with his brother. When he tried to bypass a check-point in Mahala, he went through Zivaljevina and I know that he was arrested as well as his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know his role in arming and organising Muslims in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about the role of Mehmedagic who in peacetime was the chief of the Territorial Defence and, in May, he went to his village and took up the command of a unit that was prepared?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he worked in the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he continued -- actually, he left the town immediately and took up command of units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please tell me which units and which village?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then, we have to show you his statement where all of that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to have the document admitted. We just want to show it. It's 1D04167.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just take this opportunity while the document is coming up. I know we are going to show the witness a statement of a third party and you invited me to give Dr. Karadzic advice, and I'm sorry if I'm disappointing you, but my advice to him is that it's okay to show a witness a third-party statement if he thinks that there is something in the third-party statement that could be -- elicit positive evidence from the witness and that he should put a very pointed question to the witness about the third-party statement. So I didn't want you to think that he was acting against my advice, although sometimes he doesn't do it in exactly the way that I would have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like him to put his question first and after having heard the witness's answer, and if he finds it is necessary and helpful to suggest the relevant part of the statement, then he does it, but just starting with these third parties statement outright, I don't think it helps the proceedings very much. And he spends a lot of time reading it. And reading the -- reading the statements part -- third-party statements which will not be admitted means nothing. If you could tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I told him that and I think it's important that he comes to a very small, conclusive point when he exhibits a third-party statement. I think he's attempting to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. He should understand. Let's see. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, but just to follow up on that so there is no misunderstanding. I understand the point to be that if the witness knows nothing about it, then the time spent in dwelling on the statement is useless and that's why the predicate approach suggested by the Court is far more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the witness might be more inclined to accept the assertion if they see it's part of the statement, so I would think possibly in some cases it could be more beneficial to show the statement, but we understand the Chamber's point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 5? It's probably a higher page number in e-court, probably. It's probably page 9 but at the bottom it says page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to look at the bottom where it says: "At the time no organ of power in Rogatica was functioning. I was resolving all the questions as the commander of the TO with my associates, Ajanovic Memnun, Semso Dedajic, Kasim Delic, Nermin Pisto, Osman Muhic, Emir Braulovic. I was appointed to the post at about the 15th of April, 1992, by Lutvic Adil at the time. I worked in a co-ordinated way with units in the village of Kramer Selo, Kovanj, Zepa, Kukavica, and in town with neighbourhoods Podljun and Podhrid. I was in the Zivaljevina sector where my command post was." Mr. Witness, from the 15th of April, this man had units in Kramer Selo, Kovanj, Zepa, Kukavica, and you say that you don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to comment on that. I said that I was in my own village. I was not in these other villages. I don't know what his assignments were. My village is not mentioned anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But yesterday you denied that there were any units in Kramer Selo, but now do you see that there, in fact, were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many there were because I did not go to Kramer Selo at all. I didn't stop by there at all so I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is my last warning to you. If you like to argue that what is stated -- contained in third party statements to be true, then the Prosecution could introduce tens of thousands of documents. Just please take into account what Mr. Robinson had told you. In the future, we may prohibit you from putting these third party statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am disputing here the relevance of this witness on all other matters except his incidents. He doesn't have any other evidence other than the fact that it was a theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are absolutely entitled to challenge whatever points the witness has made. But reading out a third party's statement is useless. You can put your question. And introduce this third party statement later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And do we see this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify the record. In fairness to the witness, I tried to look quickly to see whether the assertion made by the accused that the witness had specifically denied something, yesterday, was accurate, and as I read the transcript, the witness was asked if he was aware of something and he said no, I wasn't aware of that. It's quite a difference in terms of the alleged impeachment and indeed the use, the attempted use, of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the interpretation was wrong. I did not say denied. I said he didn't know. But I accept that the witness said he "nije znao" [phoen], did not know. There is a large statement with this witness. He doesn't know about a lot of things but only heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do know about the unfortunate incident that happened. So let us all now focus on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have to move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to thank you for your testimony and to say to you that I asked for more extensive information because your information contains a great deal of what you had heard. I wish to express my solidarity to you, and I would like to say how pleased I am that you survived through all of that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ607 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too. I said that I was under oath here, and I cannot speak about things that I did not see myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No questions in redirect, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you, sir. Your evidence has now been concluded. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to express our thanks to you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. But please remain seated for a while. Shall we go back to -- go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Selmanovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Ms. Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Munira Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 23rd of January, 2009; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review this statement yesterday when you prepared for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have not had an opportunity to review it. I didn't ask to be given the statement to review it, nor did anyone offer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, you said, when we spoke in the room next door, you said that you have some difficulties hearing what is said through the headphone. Is that still --

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you hear me -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness informed me that she has problems with the headphones and she would not really understand what is being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you try again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just ask you again --

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is ringing in my ears. Perhaps the volume should be put down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope this time it's better, Madam Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is better now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to come closer to the microphones, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly come closer to the microphones so that the interpreters can hear you better. Take it easy, please, Madam. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will ask you again and now I hope you can understand me better. Ms. Selmanovic, your statement of January 2009, in the English language, was it read to you while you prepared for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember that you read it to us, that we were discussing how it should be. I do remember that it was read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And can you affirm that the statement accurately reflects the information that you provided in 2009?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that I cannot tell you. I thought about it on several occasions but I never made any notes, nothing of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What you told the investigator in 2009, was that the truth? Was it correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the truth. Yes, it's true. I do need some prompting to recall these events, but when I do remember them, I do say and describe things as they were, and I did describe the events as they happened in that village of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Selmanovic. Ms. Selmanovic, would you provide the same information to the Court if you were questioned again on the same matters?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If something had not been clear to me, I would have said so. And if I do find something hard to understand, I will say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this statement, 65 ter 22600, for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the Court's permission I would now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence as admitted, as follows: Ms. Selmanovic lived with her family in the village of Novoseoci in the Sokolac municipality, a village inhabited by about 60 to 70 Muslim families. The relations with the neighbouring Serb villages were peaceful. After the outbreak of the war, the Muslim villagers were requested to hand over their weapons, such as hunting rifles, a request the villagers complied with. They were also assured that they could continue to live in Novoseoci without fear. On the 22nd of September, 1992, Novoseoci was attacked by Serb soldiers. The villagers were gathered at a meadow above the village. In the process, one female villager was killed. Soldiers looted the Muslim houses and beat the witness's father who was bed-ridden. Men and older boys were separated from the women, children and the elderly. While the latter were driven in a bus to the confrontation line from where they had to walk towards Sarajevo, 44 boys and men had to stay behind, including Ms. Selmanovic's husband and her 18-year-old son and other relatives. The body of many of the men and boys who stayed behind were later found and exhumed from a grave site in the Sokolac municipality. The body of the witness's husband wasn't found until today. Your Honour, that concludes the summary, and I have only a very few questions of you to ask, Ms. Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, in your statement, and I'll refer here to paragraphs 3 and 4, you mentioned that in spring time, villagers handed over weapons and, later on, others came to the village and also inquired about weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this context, I would like to call up Exhibit 65 ter 05384, please. And as you look on to the screen, here is a document, a record, of the confiscation of weapons in the village Novoseoci, of the 2nd Romanija Brigade dated 27 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, do you -- do you remember that as late as July, weapons were being requested?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only remember that bit about the 27th of July, around the 27th of July, and the 1st of May. And I only recall, as far as the 27th of July is concerned, that the villagers were told that they should not be concerned about their safety, that they should go on about their business, that fuel and whatever else they would need would be delivered to them from Sokolac. I remember one of the villagers saying, "Well, now we will not feel safe any longer when all our weapons are taken." But he and the others were told that they should not be concerned about their safety, that everything would be as before. And that's exactly how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you be kind -- just a second. Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now have Exhibit 65 ter 7064 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, Ms. Selmanovic, in your statement, and here I refer to paragraph 15, you describe how you took your father out of the house and that you saw soldiers plundering houses when you were doing this. And here, we have a document dated 26 September 1992, from a Commander Krstic, he gives approval to a conscript to transport furniture, appliances and kitchen equipment from Novoseoci to Sokolac. And it further says also here, the above-mentioned items will be transferred until final moving into the house in Novoseoci, which the above-named has chosen for future living. Ms. Selmanovic, what happened to your own furniture? Do you know? And all your equipment and your goods.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: My father was in the house. The soldiers told me that I should take my father out, that he shouldn't be in the house, and as we were going out, as I supported him on our way out together with a neighbour, they were already coming into the house and taking things out. And that's true. Things were taken out of the house. That's it. I lifted my father, helped him out. I left him by the road and returned up to the area where all our villagers were assembled, and I did not return to the house again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this is a proper document to be introduced through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has described how the village was looted, and this document confirms what the witness is saying. The event in Novoseoci took place on the 27th of September, and here we have a certificate or, rather, an approval by Commander Krstic allowing someone, a soldier, to remove --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Removal of looted items.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, from Novoseoci to Sokolac. Therefore I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does this document talk about the looted items?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says: "Approval to transport furniture, appliances," and so on and so forth, "from Novoseoci to Sokolac." And according to the witness's evidence, Novoseoci is a Muslim village and there is no -- it can only be from the Muslim houses. This is why I simply think that this document confirms the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll give you the floor -- before I give you the floor, Ms. Selmanovic, can you read the document? Can you tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read it, no. I can't see it properly. But tell me what it is about. I cannot read it. I am not able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it is quite unclear here how this would be transported from Novoseoci to Sokolac, when it is stated in the document that the person would be living in Novoseoci. Second of all, it is not signed by Krstic. It is stated here that it was signed on his behalf. We don't know who the person who signed was and whether it was -- the person had the authority to sign it. The translation of the document does not clearly state, as the original does, that it was signed on his behalf, for him. And not by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, would you like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could add something, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It actually is relevant because it occurred yesterday when Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was not in the courtroom, and it was in connection with the guidelines for admission of such documents. And that involved the question of context and authenticity. And in relation to that discussion, it should be clear, and I believe the Court will remember from yesterday, that the testimony of this witness and in this document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember this specific thing and Krstic and who carried it. I only saw them carry the items out of my house and I remember going back to the point where we were all assembled. I said that there was this person who ordered that we should leave, but I don't know who came when we left and looted the area. I know that I took my father out and I waited by, that's all. It was looting, but there were several soldiers there taking things out of the homes, flour and pieces of furniture, and I'm talking about my house. I couldn't see what was going on in the other homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As it happens the witness's comments amply buttress the point I wanted to make, which was we talked about two factors, in that case it was context, I think it's very clear that this document is amply contextualised by the evidence of this witness. And once context has been fulfilled, it is as here, the remaining, as question we discussed yesterday, was whether there was any question about the authenticity of the document. This is classically the kind of document that has been admitted. The factors identified by Dr. Karadzic may go to weight but not to the authenticity of the document, and this is one which fulfils both of the requirements that have been developed during the course of these proceedings for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we have a problem. The witness's admission -- the admission of the witness that she cannot read, she is not able to read, how would she be able to identify any documents put to her? Is there a method you could use?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did that also in the proofing already, what we simply did, we read it to her. We always read each document that I today present to you, and there is one more coming, we basically read it to her. So we could -- I could, for instance, read what is written here to her -- here into the record so that she doesn't need to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps you can could that just to ensure that this statement she has made is put in proper context. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, I'll read to you now the text of this document that is in front of you and it says: "Command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade," and then there is a number. And then: "Sokolac, 26 September 1992." And the text of the document says: "Approval. This is to certify that conscript Dragomir Bozic, from the 2nd Romanija Mountain Brigade, has received approval to transport furniture, appliances, a fridge, a cooking stove, a washing machine, chairs, two beds, and a freezer from Novoseoci to Sokolac. "The above-mentioned items will be transferred until final moving into a house in Novoseoci, which the above-named has chosen for future living." And it says here, "Commander, Colonel Radisav Krstic," and then there is a signature that, as Mr. Karadzic pointed out, is not from Mr. Krstic. That's what the document basically says.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I can tell you in response to this. Everything you mention, including Krstic, I can't tell you who took the things away. I can only tell you that they gathered all the villagers, myself included, in a meadow and I was ordered to go to my house and take my father out. Meanwhile, they were carrying things out of the house. Was it Krstic? Who was it? I don't know. But things including the fridges, and everything else, were being taken out of my house. And of course I can't tell you if anybody moved into the house later on or not. They boarded us on a bus with children, but our men were left behind. From then on, I don't know. I don't know who took it, was it Krstic, somebody else. At any rate, everything, at least as far as my house is concerned, what I saw was taken out of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I had help my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the interpreter could be kind enough to read what is written in the stamp. I can read the first one, "Vojna."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Military post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the middle, it says "Sokolac"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you know that Mr. Krstic was located in Sokolac at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would assume it from the document, but I would have to look at a lot of other documents to confirm this now 100 per cent, but it looks like it. At least was in the region as a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Romanija Motorised Brigade was located in Sokolac. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I may have been of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can speak when you're given the floor. This time the Chamber does not need your assistance. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, the Chamber is not satisfied that this document as such is contextually related to the looting that the witness is referring to. So the witness's testimony is in the transcript and you will have another opportunity to introduce this document into evidence. Or maybe by bar table motion, but we will see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will not admit this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I have one more document to discuss with the witness. Can we please have 65 ter 22869 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, in your statement, and I refer here to paragraph 22, you refer to the exhumation from a grave site in Ivan Polje. Do you recall when this exhumation took place?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 2000, around September or October. I don't know the exact date but it was in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you attend it? Did you watch what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were called to attend over three days. That's how long it took. It's a valley, Ivan Polje. In the area left of the valley, we knew that a mosque had been situated there so we thought that that's where it would be. They were working in the area for three days but it was only on the fourth that they recovered bodies, including the bones of my son. It was a pit, and there they called us villagers to go and see what they found because there was some clothing there. There were three bodies in this pit and I immediately recognised my child because I saw the sweater and his necklace. And then they moved these little bones belonging to our children, asking us this and that, is it him, and I said of course. First they showed us the bodies up front, and then from the back. There I was able to see bullets coming out of the remains. I saw my son in a sweater and his hand lying peacefully, and then I realised it was him. And I survived that ordeal as well, but it was my child. I recognised him. That's exactly how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you see in front of you is the exhumation report related to the exhumation of this particular grave that the witness just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall that you, basically, with the help of an interpreter, went through the names in that document, the names of the people exhumed? Do you recall that, that you did that yesterday? Or the day before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember. All the names are there. All the people there are found. Later everybody recognised their own. When we were called to go to identify them, I did not identify my husband, and my relative among those 40 or so. Their bodies were not there. I looked at the names of the sons, the fathers and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't think Defence will object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will tender it. And this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will give the number to the exhumation report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P3297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Madam Selmanovic, you'll be further asked by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before we proceed, I would just rise to a brief scheduling issue at the request of the pro se office. They had anticipated commencing the interviews we spoke about earlier at 2.00. There is a one-hour transportation period. They understand expressly that they are -- that the Court's schedule will dictate the timing of the videolinks, but they did want to know definitively whether the Court was going to adjourn now and postpone the cross or to continue and conclude the witness and then pro se should move the videolinks back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before making any decision, how long do you think you will take, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I'm waiting for the interpretation. It's taking a long time. Your Excellencies, I will do my best to finish within an hour but I'm afraid that it would be difficult in view of the circumstances. It will be difficult to get the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your estimate is you can finish -- you cannot finish in an hour's time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid not. I will do my best. I will try my best but I'm not sure that I will succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no point of postponing this witness's cross-examination to next week and we will proceed. The point of my question was whether you need all of that one hour. I was of the opinion that you could finish much quicker. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Selmanovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to express my sympathy and solidarity because of your loss, and now I would like to ask you to help me shed some light on some things. I'm going to start from this last thing that you said, and that is that at the place where the location -- the exhumation took place, it was a cemetery and there was a mosque there before?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a cemetery. It was a valley, which is where they threw our people who were captured by Pajic. Let me tell you that. They took them for a work drive and then they just left them there. I blame Pajic alone for what he did and for what was done. That Pajic took our children and our fathers and our husbands, ranging in age from 15 to 80. And then he left them all on the work drive and then he took them to this Ivan Polje valley. I don't know if they are there or not, in that valley, are there -- later that the rubble from the cemetery was thrown on top of them, and then it took three days for them to go through all of that rubble to be able to find the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? Start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said you mentioned the mosque today for the first time, and that's why I asked. And I kindly ask you, wherever possible, to answer with a "yes" or a "no" so that we could finish as soon as possible. You said today that you recognised him by his necklace.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised him by his necklace, by his clothes, by his footwear, by his bones. I recognise my own child and everybody else recognised their own child. I went there. I was called to go to Ivan Polje three times. I went all around, the first day, the second day, the third day, I went around. There was this commission from Sokolac. They were saying they are not there, they are not there, they are not there. Then the earth diggers began to find things. Then when we found that, they cleaned it. Then they called us, they brought us there. They lined up the bodies in these bags or something. I don't know. They put them on something, bags or something, and then as people were approaching, I immediately recognised my own child by his clothing. But they said, Please don't touch anything with your hands. We didn't touch anything. They took him and they turned him over, and then I could see that it was my child. I don't know what was done, I don't know if it was done because of Pajic, by his will or whoever, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that there were clothes and footwear, that there was clothing and shoes and that it wasn't destroyed or didn't -- wasn't disintegrating?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't disintegrating. There was a woollen sweater. It was whole. And you could see in the front where the bullet had gone through, but when they turned the body on the back, you could see nothing. And he had shoes on his feet and you could see the bones inside these shoes. There was a belt. There was a jacket with some threads on it, and the sweater was complete and whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was there a different stage of decomposition of the bodies? Were the bodies in different stages of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody recognised their own. There was nothing different about the bodies. Each recognised their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that a number of bullets fell, a number of shells fell off the body.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the body of my child, seven shell casings dropped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to go back to the beginning. In the spring of 1992, you asked the Serbian authorities in Sokolac to allow you to evacuate the village and they talked you out of it, or rather, they persuaded you to stay; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was requested, and they were coming from Sokolac and they were encouraging people, Look, you know, there is no need for you to go. You're not under any danger. We will come and we will inform you. And until the 1st of May, people were working in their companies. Later there were holidays. Later they came, took away the weapons, this was on the 27th. And then one man said, You know, when you took these things, then for us it's no longer safe to live here. He said, It's safe. There is no need. Why aren't you working? They said, Well, we don't have any fuel, we don't have anything, we cannot operate the machinery. Then they said, Well, you can go to Sokolac now, you can buy the fuel, you can continue to work. There will be no problem. This is what they told the men. They didn't tell the women that. They told the men and the men told us. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is 65 ter 22604 on page 1, it's in a statement given by Ms. Selmanovic earlier, that they were going to request the evacuation of the village and that they were talked out of it. Did you say that Drago Macar also came and that others would come and tell you that you should stay; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. Drago Macar came first and he said, There is no need, you should stay. And then later Velimir Elez and Savic Milorad came, they said, There is no need, people, just go and get the fuel, and they went immediately with their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the weapons were handed over and this happened on three occasions, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the third time. I know about the two occasions. This was on the 27th and then on the 1st of May. I'm not sure about the dates, to be able to say it was on such and such a date. This was in the spring in May, and this was around the 27th, it could have been a day or two before. People continued to harvest, cut the crops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in your statement 22604, for other participants, it says on the 6th of July, 1992, again weapons were handed over, some weapons. Why didn't they hand in all the weapons in one go?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because they didn't have any. What are they going to hand over? Whoever had something, they handed it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 5385? I'm convinced there is a translation. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is actually an exhibit that I first also considered to use and we have a translation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this has been admitted. Probably under different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The 65 ter number that Mr. Karadzic mentioned is correct. I have it here with me as well, and I have a translation. Mr. Reid is uploading it right now. It was not uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, while we are waiting for the English translation I'm going to read to you a sentence which refers to Novoseoci. This is the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the date is the 27th of July and it's informing the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it states: "In the village of Novoseoci, south of Sokolac" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You're reading from this document. The interpreter is asking for a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the last third of the first paragraph, "In the village of Novoseoci." This is how it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat: "In the village of Novoseoci, south of Sokolac, some five to six kilometres, Glasinacko Polje, weapons were handed over, as well as lethal equipment, by the Muslim population to representatives of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. The hand-over was carried out per agreement but it is believed that all of the weapons were not handed over." This is the second or the third time but you think that it was the second time, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that on the 27th this Pajic came and that Velimir Elez came and that this is what was said, and that he asked and people gave what they had. And what you're talking about, killings and all of this, probably had they had them they would have given them, probably people didn't have them, and then they were promised that they should stay, and they offered some kind of assurance, and they stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this and can we now again have 22604, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that it is a very similar case to the previous one but the Prosecution would not have an objection to it because it does fit into the -- what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the submission of Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1667, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I'm wondering, speaking for myself, whether there is any point of going through the documents with this witness, Mr. Karadzic, given the short -- given the time. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm going to just limit myself to the statements by the witness and she will remember that. Can we have this 65 ter 22604, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to read you the second sentence of the statement: "Sometime in early June, our villages, Mustafa Selmanovic, Hilmija Karic and Lutvo Ocuz went to see Romanija -- Djokic Slavko on Mount Romanija regarding the potential evacuation of our village because even though there was no threat, we were becoming concerned that our village would be attacked by some Arkan's or Seselj's men from Serbia" and so on and so forth. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I am not aware of that. Nobody was going anywhere. People were working until the 1st of May. On the 1st of May we were given holidays. They said we would summon you back to work. Nobody went anywhere. And as I told you, these people were stopping by, Macar, Savic, Velimir, all of those people came as well as Rade Dubovina, who used to come by practically every day, and he would be talking to people, People, there is no need, it's like this, like that. I've told you everything. And as for Mustafa, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you mentioned Pero Dubovina and Rade Dubovina in that paragraph. You say that they came and that they were convincing you that you could stay?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned Rade Dubovina, the son of Ljubo Dubovina, he came to the village until that time when they were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, you mentioned that they came to Bogovici on the 6th or 7th, Milorad Savic and others, and that they just wanted weapons to be handed over and to have money changed for Serbian money.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not mention Bogovici at all. I didn't mention any of that to you. As for these bank notes, I mean through these people who talked to their people, they said, Go and change that money, these bank notes. As for Bogovici, no, no. These people who came, like Rade Dubovina and -- they said, Go and change it, don't spend this. They spent that money of theirs and then they come to our village, what do you need? And that was that. They were doing something that was supposed to be some kind of favour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting question in relation to a document, in particular it is a statement of the witness, I would like you to explain to the witness the nature of the document, what you're going -- which you are going to put to her. But I --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. After this question. On the second page, the witness's signature is missing. So you have to put everything to the witness and proceed. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And perhaps also a caution to be very careful with mentioning the names. Basically saying it very clearly because I got always the impression that the witness didn't get the name Jolovic, proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, this is a statement that you gave on the 11th of January, 1993. Did you give a statement to some Jusuf Begic in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you I do not remember. I didn't write down any dates or who I gave statements to. I was giving statements but my soul was in pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that near your village, there were some armed Muslim villages that were fighting, shooting and had units of their own, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any of that either because we weren't moving anywhere. We were in our own village. These people came and said what they said, and I don't know about any of what you said now or these surrounding villages and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you said a moment ago, that people were doing things that were supposed to be a favour to these villages, was it these, the Serb authorities from Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: All of them are from Sokolac. First Savic, then Milorad Savic, and this other person said all right, come with us, buy fuel, work with machines, buy what you need, all of that is correct. Then they would come to some village, bring whatever was needed, people would take that. There you go, that's how it was. These were these favours done by the people of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But there was shooting nevertheless. In this same statement on page 2, you said that on the 27th of July there were some strong gunfire from all weapons there and then you were asked to hand over weapons. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not the way it was. That is not the way it was. These people came to tell people that it was good for them to stay. We women did not even walk up there. It was the men who were talking. Nobody was attacking the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There weren't any attacks against the village?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no attacks against the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When they came on the 22nd of September also there were no attacks, you just happened to notice them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that it just happened that way. It was the 22nd, at day break, we were supposed to do something. As people started getting up, they made them go out to the meadow. As we walked out of the houses, soldiers were standing in front of the houses and they just sent us to the meadow. First my child was taken prisoner and then my husband went out to see where the child was, and then I also followed him and then my brother-in-law and then my sister-in-law, there were about six of us there, and there were soldiers all around us. And then there were six of us there and my children were not there. I mean that first child of mine went, I asked where is this child? At Mican Jolovic's. Why at Mican Jolovic's? That is on the other side. I mean, these are two villages facing each other. And he said don't worry, now your child is going to be up there at that meadow, you're all going to be at that meadow. And that's the way it was. And then these soldiers took us to this meadow and then all of us villagers were there, on that meadow, and once all the villagers were there, on that meadow, this man took out this paper and this Pajic Momcilo was reading out all these names and saying are all the villagers there and then they said all but one. And I'm sorry, our children were threatened. And they said all the villagers have to be there, and if they don't come there, then they -- then you're going to be killed. The children were afraid and then we all went out for the sake of our children. And then this woman was not there and then was killed along the way. And then we were there, and then now Momcilo Pajic read this out, You know what, there are weapons and your village's houses are going to be searched. And the villagers said, No, no, which is exactly the way it was. We had handed over what was there. And we said no. And then I'm telling you, you know what, they said now we will wait, and he has that hand-held radio and he's calling Kopito [phoen]. And then he says, All right, I'm going to Sokolac, now I know we are going to see what your fate is going to be. And then Pajic Momcilo returned from Sokolac and said to us, You know what, children, women, those who cannot move, there is going to be a bus that's going to come and you're going to go by the mosque, and all of those who are capable of working are going to stay here for a work drive. Then we were in panic for our children and then the house and whatever, and then they were sending us away with these rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, may I just ask you something? Why did the children go and get the horses?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: They went because of their own needs. They wanted to work. We wanted to work. Before that, they were taking firewood to a man, Hazim, and this nephew of mine, and then they wanted to take some firewood to that man too, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To take firewood and to be paid for that, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because in the statement that somebody seemed to have worded, it seems that it was different, but actually they were doing this for money.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, everything was nice and peaceful. I cannot remember the name of this person now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This late Devla?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The wife of this man who was missing?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: She quarrelled with some woman as to who would go and get her husband and she set out, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, first they sent the daughter-in-law and the daughter-in-law said that she could not leave her children and then she said all right I'm going to get my husband. And she went to get her husband. Then she was killed below the mosque, and unfortunately, she also had her throat slit and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that, Madam, or did you see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: We saw that when they brought her opposite the mosque. We saw her lying in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said, Madam, that she walked a bit faster, that she hurried a bit and that's when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, she hurried a bit. She just wanted to cross over something. I mean there was this fence, and then you had to step over it. So that's all. It's not that she was running. I mean, if you're sent somewhere to do something, you'd run too. I mean you would hurry too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's very important for us, Madam. If she was running, then somebody from afar interpreted that as meaning that she was trying to flee. You said that in your statement, that she hurried a bit and that that's when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe, maybe she did hurry a bit. I'm telling you right now the woman wanted to cross this fence there near the mosque and that's where she was killed. You know, when you jump over something, that's when she was killed. I mean, how can I know how she was moving there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you said that you did not see that moment. You saw her body afterwards but you did not see that moment.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: While we were all gathered up there, Nail hadn't even come there, her husband, there was only this one thing that was heard and then all the soldiers jumped up and pointed their rifles at us. Since Nail came, he said, Unfortunately, my Devla has been killed. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, and then when they took us to the buses, then this body was brought to our old cemetery and then it was placed on the blanket. And her daughter-in-law walked up and saw her lying in blood and said that she had had her throat slit. There you go. What else can I say to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not see it. She said that to you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: She said that but then we also saw it. We saw it. We saw her lying in blood and that that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement, 22603, it says that Veljko Papic asked to have firewood brought to him but we have clarified the matter. That was paid for.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. And my child wanted to go that morning too. I mean, we need to make money, don't we? And it's free for us to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before this happened, your daughter and son-in-law freely went to Sarajevo through Serb territory, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: They went, I think in April, March, April, through Serb territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Banja Lucica, Kaljina and these other villages are?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know where Kaljina is, but Banja Lucica, no, never. I never went there but I went to Kaljina when I was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you know that Banja Lucica is also in your municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it is or if it isn't. I mean, I don't really understand if Kaljina is in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, then, they took you on buses to an area close to the front line and then you crossed over to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in 1993, you gave a statement and you mentioned all the things that stayed behind in Sokolac, things of yours, and you asked for compensation, you asked for damages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe I did ask for that. I mean, I'm asking even now to be compensated and to get damages. Everything was destroyed, land, houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said then that there was a refrigerator in your house and furniture.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: And my soul, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said then that you had your furniture in your house and other things. You did not mention that they had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean I didn't mention it? I said that as I came to get my father, everything was being taken out, the refrigerators, and the couches, all of that was being carried out. I mean what more can I say? I mean what do you mean did I say, did I not say? Of course, I said it. I wanted to get my father out of the house and then I saw that everything was buried and everything was being moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you did not know that your family members had been killed. Do you know when these two were killed, the two that you know of? When did that happen and in what situation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know in what situation, immediately or whatever. But we women, children, we were walking around, we went to Sokolac and we started going say in 1997 or 1998. Wherever we asked people, everyone said to us, It was the army that took them away. And we say, Which army? We just know who stopped our people and who made us board buses. I mean what kind of soldiers, I don't know that. In which direction? And they say, well, maybe it's this Ledena Pecina or Novakova Pecina. Do you know where Novakova Pecina is? All right. And then I thought perhaps sometimes we went there for picnics. So that's the way it was until we found that particle of the mosque, because all of us women were in front of the mosque and we were afraid and we were thinking about this and it couldn't have been anything else. That was that. We were looking and no one wanted to tell us where they were, as we were asking for our own. We even asked villagers and they said, Why are you asking us? They are down there, underneath that board. And the old cemetery of ours was totally dug up and the stones were taken away and they built barracks there. And they said, Well, that's where your old cemetery is now. And we said, Well, yeah, but where are the villagers now, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. But you don't know, you never found out when they were killed and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: We never found out under what circumstances or was it the same day or was it the next day. That is the only thing that the person who left them there can tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm speaking I know for myself, but I am wondering what is the point of this line of cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the last question, Excellency. I just wanted to see whether she had any knowledge as to what had happened with the men. The women and children were evacuated. I just wanted to know what happened to the men, whether she knew about that because until this indictment I had never heard of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Selmanovic. I have no further questions for you. Rest assured, Ms. Selmanovic, that all my friends and all of those who respect me and all of those who are my followers are never going to harm a single witness or any witness's family. That has never happened until now and this is a public recommendation to respect all witnesses, especially those who are victims.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I say here publicly as well, let this person who gathered us all together, who separated our children and our husbands and men and let him just say whether he did it of his own free will or did he do it for the love of you or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Selmanovic. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Selmanovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home. But you can wait. Unless there is any other matters to raise, we will rise for the week. And we will resume next week on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a sitting day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was mistaken. Yes, tomorrow at 9.00. Wishful thinking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think you should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will rise until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of September 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.41 p.m.,
